news_drafts.headline: Nottinghamshire schools-grant deficit forecast at £178m as auditor reports "significant weakness"
news_drafts.lead:
Nottinghamshire County Council's cumulative deficit on the dedicated schools grant, the government grant that funds schools, was £39.8m at 31 March 2026. Its external auditor's annual report says it is forecast to rise by £138.2m to £178m by March 2028, before government support. The auditor has determined a "significant weakness" in the council's financial sustainability arrangements, relating to the deficit. The papers go to the Audit and Governance Committee on 25 November.

The deficit sits in high needs, the part of school funding for children with special educational needs and disabilities. The paper says demand rose in 2025/26, "including a 400% rise in new referrals". The council has received £35.8m of High Needs Stability Grant, covering 90% of the high needs deficit to the end of 2025/26. It was notified in November that its Local SEND Reform Plan, submitted to the Department for Education on 19 June 2026, had passed scrutiny. A reserve of around £4m was set aside in 2025/26 for the remainder. After the grant, the auditor's completion report says the council could face a £142m residual deficit. It says this would be a significant threat to usable reserves, the part of its reserves a council can spend. That report dates the £178m forecast to 31 March 2029 in one place and to 2027/28 in another.

The statutory override, a temporary government rule keeping such deficits off the main balance sheet, expires in March 2028. The council has decided to retain reserves previously set aside to balance its budget over the medium term, which will be available to offset the high needs deficit. The auditor recommends it monitor its reform plan and assess different funding scenarios for when the override ends.

news_drafts.headline: Nottinghamshire to receive £35.8m in November for schools deficit; high needs forecast £68.8m over
news_drafts.lead:
Nottinghamshire County Council has been notified that government funding covering 90% of its dedicated schools grant (DSG) deficit at 31 March 2026 will be paid in November 2026. The sum is £35.8m, against a DSG deficit of £39.8m at the end of 2025/26. The DSG is the government grant that funds schools, and a deficit on it is an overspend on that grant. The council's Financial Monitoring Report says confirmation came after its SEND Reform Plan was submitted.

The same report, for period 5 of 2026/27, forecasts a £68.8m overspend for the year on the high needs block, the part of school funding for children with special educational needs and disabilities (SEND). The forecast is £207.7m of spending against a high needs budget of £138.9m. The paper says the underlying position continues to deteriorate, citing sustained demand and cost pressures in SEND services.

The council's Budget Update Report, also before Cabinet on 5 November, says arrangements for deficits arising in 2026/27 and 2027/28 have not yet been confirmed. It expects further announcements before the end of March 2028. It says continuation of 90% support cannot currently be assumed. If it is not sustained, the remaining 10%, £6.9m of the forecast 2026/27 high needs deficit, would have to be met from the council's reserves.

news_drafts.headline: Nottinghamshire: Ombudsman found fault in seven SEND cases as EHC Plan numbers rose 27% in a year
news_drafts.lead:
The Local Government and Social Care Ombudsman, the independent body that investigates complaints about councils, found fault in seven cases involving Nottinghamshire County Council's special educational needs and disabilities (SEND) service between March and September 2026. The decisions are set out in a paper for the council's Audit and Governance Committee, which meets on 14 October.

The paper describes the faults as systematic. They mainly concerned a failure to secure the support written into Education, Health and Care (EHC) Plans, the legal documents setting out what help a child with special needs must receive. Other faults were delays in the plan process and missed educational provision. In the paper's words: "A recurring theme was the failure to ensure that agreed educational or therapeutic provision was delivered. This included missed special school placements, physiotherapy, occupational therapy, music therapy, communication aids (AAC), and wider EHC provision."

Over the same period the number of EHC Plans in Nottinghamshire grew to just under 7,000, a rise of 27% on the previous year.

findings.paper_title: Treasury Management Mid-Year Report 2026-27 Appendix A
findings.headline: Council's internal borrowing stood at £266m at the start of 2026/27, up from £251m in 2025/26.
findings.detail: The paper describes internal borrowing as using cash-backed earmarked reserves, the general fund reserve and working capital to fund capital expenditure before the cash is needed for its earmarked purpose.
findings.matters: A higher level of internal borrowing shows how far a council is relying on its own cash to fund capital, and how much external borrowing it is deferring.
findings.figures: £266m internal borrowing at start of 2026/27; £251m at start of 2025/26
findings.quote: At the beginning of 2026/27 the Council’s internal borrowing stood at £266m (£251m in 2025/26).

findings.paper_title: Treasury Management Mid-Year Report 2026-27 Appendix A
findings.headline: Council earned £1.627m in interest in the half-year to September, a 3.90% average rate of return against an average adjusted SONIA of 3.61%.
findings.detail: The paper benchmarks cash returns against SONIA, which is the council's stated policy. The council's return was above the adjusted SONIA benchmark over the same period.
findings.matters: Finance officers at other councils can compare their own return against the SONIA benchmark used by this council.
findings.figures: £1.627m interest earned; 3.90% average rate of return; 3.61% average adjusted SONIA
findings.quote: Over the same period the average adjusted SONIA was 3.61%.

findings.paper_title: Treasury Management Mid-Year Report 2026-27 Appendix A
findings.headline: Council's mid-year cash balance was approximately £46m, against £103m at the same point in 2025/26.
findings.detail: The paper attributes the lower balance to cash generally being lower in 2026/27. All deposits were placed in instant-access money market funds, with no fixed-term loans to banks or local authorities, so the council can defer borrowing.
findings.matters: A fall in cash balances of this size means less internal borrowing capacity and a greater need for external funding, which other councils and lenders will want to track.
findings.quote: The Council’s mid-year cash balance was approximately £ 46m (the corresponding figure for 2025/26 was £103m).

findings.paper_title: Treasury Management Mid-Year Report 2026-27 Appendix A
findings.headline: Council took on £20m of new PWLB debt in August-September 2026 and repaid £7.1m of maturing PWLB debt in May, with a further £10.2m due in November.
findings.detail: The paper reports these PWLB movements in the first half of the year and estimates a further £90m of borrowing is required. Forecast long-term debt at 31 March 2027 is £522.8m, within an operational boundary of £533m and an authorised limit of £558m.
findings.matters: A finance director elsewhere can compare the scale of new PWLB drawdown and the forecast year-end debt against the council's prudential limits.
findings.figures: £20m new PWLB debt; £7.1m repaid May; £10.2m maturing November; £90m further borrowing required; £522.8m forecast debt at 31 March 2027; £533m operational boundary; £558m authorised limit
findings.quote: £20m of new PWLB debt was taken on during August-September.

findings.paper_title: Treasury Management Mid-Year Report 2026-27 Appendix A
findings.headline: Council redeemed a £10m LOBO loan in April 2026 and again in June, after lenders opted to increase rates above the prevailing PWLB rate, clearing all LOBO debt from its books.
findings.detail: The paper reports that the lenders chose to raise the interest rate above the prevailing PWLB rate, and the council redeemed the loan rather than accept it. The two redemptions cleared all LOBO debt from the council's books. The paper does not give the coupon, the proposed rate, the lender's name, or the cost of replacement funding.
findings.matters: Every LOBO call is a repayment and replacement event, and the paper shows Nottinghamshire has now removed its LOBO exposure entirely, which changes its refinancing and interest-rate risk profile.
findings.figures: £10m redeemed in April 2026 and again in June; PWLB rate referenced but not quantified
findings.quote: The Council redeemed a £10m ‘LOBO’ loan in April 2026 and again in June, as the lenders opted to increase interest rates above the prevailing PWLB rate.

daily_post.headline: The suspension rate for pupils with an EHCP is 40.5%, compared with 26.5% nationally.
daily_post.lead: SEND suspension and exclusion rates are a demand and cost driver for high-needs budgets, and councils facing the same pressures can compare these national benchmarks directly.
